"Instantly" vs. "Instantaneously"
I'm wondering what the difference is between these two words. This has been mulling around in the back of my head for a few months now, and I realize that this all might sound incredibly frivolous, but just try to bear with me...

A big part of what makes this so confusing to me is that each dictionary and article I've looked at have shared a lot of the same terms in there definitions, but use them interchangeably as if they're synonymous, so I just get more confused the more I look into it.

Despite that, I decided it would be best to cite from Merriam-Webster:

**Instantly:**

>1 : with importunity

>2 : without the least delay

**Instantaneously:**

>1 : done, occurring, or acting without any perceptible duration of time

>2 : done without any delay being purposely introduced

>3 : occurring or present at a particular instant

These definitions seem to overlap and contradict each other. "Instantaneously" is described as, *"acting without any perceptible duration of time"*, while "instantly" is not; so the only difference it seems is that "instantaneously" is faster(?) than "instantly" because, as per the definition, no delay is perceptible. However, such a definition seems arbitrary. But on the other hand, the definition for "instantly", as I understand it, is defined as being an immediate action as well (which sounds exactly how "instantaneously" is described)...

I just don't understand... Personally, I feel like one of these words should just get the boot because they mean the same freaking thing. The only thing separating the two is purely semantics. However, that's just my opinion, if one of you could explain this to me it would be greatly appreciated.
